units.title: Unit 35 — Social issues
learningObjectives: Use idiomatic collocations to discuss social problems, civic responses and public order.
Recognise housing and neighbourhood language relevant to inequality, safety and welfare.
Distinguish formal policy expressions, metaphors and emotionally charged descriptions.
Apply accurate verb–noun pairings for appeals, relief, change and community initiatives.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The commission intends to address an issue that has been ignored for years.
items.note: Address an issue means take steps to consider or deal with it, not necessarily resolve it.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Large-scale economic migration has changed the population of several industrial cities.
items.note: Large-scale describes scope; economic migration refers to movement motivated by livelihood prospects.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Community volunteers can become a force for good when institutions are overstretched.
items.note: A force for good is a person or influence that produces beneficial change.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The housing cooperative proposed a novel solution to the shortage of small apartments.
items.note: Novel means new or original in this formal collocation, not connected with fiction.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Local councils must tackle a problem before it becomes a regional crisis.
items.note: Tackle a problem means confront it actively; solving it is not guaranteed.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Several charities joined forces to provide relief after the severe flooding.
items.note: Provide relief is common for humanitarian assistance in emergencies.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The mayor announced a fresh drive to improve safety around schools.
items.note: A fresh drive is a renewed organised effort to achieve a goal.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The local doctor made a plea for safer pedestrian crossings.
items.note: Make a plea is an urgent request; do not use do a plea.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Support programmes can help families break the cycle of persistent poverty.
items.note: Break the cycle means interrupt a repeating and damaging pattern.

items.word: a breakdown of law and order
items.pt: um colapso da lei e da ordem
items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Residents feared a breakdown of law and order during the prolonged unrest.
items.note: A breakdown of law and order means that institutions can no longer maintain public safety and order.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Officials closed the main square after riots erupted in neighbouring districts.
items.note: Erupt conveys a sudden outbreak; a riot is a violent public disturbance.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The city introduced a mediation service to reduce incidents of public disorder.
items.note: Public disorder refers to disturbances of public peace, often involving crowds.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Long-term isolation can weaken the social fabric of small communities.
items.note: Social fabric metaphorically refers to relationships and structures holding society together.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Several rights groups criticised the proposed draconian measures as disproportionate.
items.note: Draconian describes excessively harsh or severe measures, usually critically.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The council prioritised repairs in run-down areas near the old railway line.
items.note: Run-down describes neglected, deteriorating places; do not confuse it with run out.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The residents worked with youth workers to prevent antisocial behaviour in the park.
items.note: Antisocial behaviour disrupts or harms other people; common in British public-policy English.

items.pt: consumo de álcool por menores de idade
items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The campaign focuses on reducing underage drinking during holiday festivals.
items.note: Underage drinking means consuming alcohol before the legal minimum age.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: Counsellors sometimes support children growing up in dysfunctional families.
items.note: Dysfunctional describes family relationships that do not function healthily; use sensitively.

items.pt: passar a ser examinado de perto
items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The contractor came under scrutiny after repeated safety complaints.
items.note: Come under scrutiny means become subject to close investigation or critical examination.

items.section: A · Facing and solving social problems
items.example: The spending proposal received intense scrutiny from independent auditors.
items.note: Intense scrutiny emphasises the depth or severity of examination.

items.example: The programme reserves a portion of its homes for low-income families.
items.note: Low-income modifies a person or group with relatively little income; hyphenate before nouns.

items.example: Emergency teams opened a school gym to provide shelter overnight.
items.note: Provide shelter means offer a safe place to stay, usually temporarily.

items.example: Inspectors reported poor sanitary conditions in the temporary accommodation.
items.note: Sanitary conditions concern hygiene, water and waste disposal; poor means inadequate.

items.example: The inspection found the basement unfit for human habitation because of mould.
items.note: A formal expression for accommodation too unsafe or unhealthy to live in.

items.example: The redevelopment plan includes affordable housing for essential workers.
items.note: Affordable housing concerns homes priced within the financial reach of intended residents.

items.example: The moderator removed messages that appeared to incite violence against protesters.
items.note: Incite means encourage others to commit violence; it is stronger than discuss violence.

items.example: The proposed harsh punishment prompted debate about proportionality.
items.note: Harsh punishment stresses severity and often implies criticism of the penalty.

items.example: Residents created a neighbourhood watch scheme with support from the local police.
items.note: A British-English name for coordinated community crime-prevention efforts.

items.example: The council plans to introduce a scheme offering temporary rent support.
items.note: Introduce a scheme means establish a new organised policy or programme.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: The security team discovered an illegal substance in the abandoned storeroom.
items.note: A formal or euphemistic description, often used for drugs controlled by law.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: Eligible residents can claim benefits through the local welfare office.
items.note: In UK English, claim benefits refers to applying for or receiving state support.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: The coalition hopes to become a force for change in regional transport policy.
items.note: A force for change creates pressure or momentum for reform; change need not be positive.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: The youth movement demanded political change through peaceful elections.
items.note: Political change is a broad noun phrase about shifts in institutions or policies.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: The foundation funded research to address social inequality in education.
items.note: Address inequality means make a deliberate attempt to reduce or deal with it.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: Households affected by the closure could claim financial support from the relief fund.
items.note: Claim means formally request what one may be eligible to receive.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: Event organisers collaborated with officials to prevent public disorder after the match.
items.note: Prevent disorder means act before a disturbance occurs.

items.section: C · Social policy and civic action
items.example: Faith leaders made a plea for tolerance during the community meeting.
items.note: A plea for something specifies the cause or behaviour the speaker urgently requests.

units.title: Unit 36 — Science and technology
learningObjectives: Use research and engineering collocations to explain discoveries, practical applications and system failures.
Distinguish shutdown, loss of power, data loss and normal wear in technology contexts.
Describe everyday digital services and devices with natural lexical combinations.
Interpret figurative and contextual meanings of remote, screen, online and scientific findings.

items.word: push back the frontiers of knowledge
items.example: Joint research teams aim to push back the frontiers of knowledge in materials science.
items.note: A metaphor for extending what is known; push back the frontiers takes of plus a field.

items.example: The team expects to publish findings after independent reviewers examine its methods.
items.note: Findings is ordinarily plural when it means research results; avoid singular finding here.

items.example: The sensor technology has promising commercial applications in industrial monitoring.
items.note: Commercial applications are practical uses marketed or deployed in business.

items.example: Small farms are learning to harness technology to improve water management.
items.note: Harness technology means use its power or capabilities for a practical purpose.

items.example: The new laboratory introduced cutting-edge design into its measurement equipment.
items.note: Cutting-edge is a compound adjective meaning highly advanced or innovative.

items.example: The pilot should run smoothly once the remaining compatibility issues are resolved.
items.note: Run smoothly refers to an operation proceeding without interruptions or difficulties.

items.example: A specialist will install equipment in the control room on Friday.
items.note: Install means put hardware in place and make it ready for use.

items.example: Regular inspections help detect wear and tear in the moving parts.
items.note: Wear and tear means deterioration through normal repeated use, not sudden damage.

items.example: Engineers investigated why the backup systems crashed during the stress test.
items.note: Crash describes a sudden computer or system failure, not a planned shutdown.

items.example: You could lose data if the recorder shuts down before saving the session.
items.note: Lose data is a common phrase for files or information being deleted or rendered unavailable.

items.example: A brief power cut interrupted the automated packaging line.
items.note: In British English, power cut means an interruption of electricity supply.

items.example: Technicians worked through the night to restore power to the clinic.
items.note: Restore power means bring the supply back after an outage.

items.example: A defective valve forced the factory to halt production for several hours.
items.note: Halt production means stop manufacturing, often temporarily and unexpectedly.

items.example: Always shut down a computer properly before replacing internal components.
items.note: Shut down refers to closing processes and turning off the machine, not merely locking the screen.

items.example: The presentation began late because of technical problems with the projector.
items.note: Technical problems are faults related to equipment, systems or specialised operation.

items.example: The research group will carry out research on alternative battery materials.
items.note: Research is uncountable in this sense; use some research, not researches.

items.example: The grant supports pure research with no immediate product requirement.
items.note: Pure research pursues knowledge for its own sake, unlike applied development.

items.example: The company hopes to apply research to practical projects in rural healthcare.
items.note: Apply research to a problem means use findings in a concrete setting.

items.example: The award recognised a scientific discovery that challenged earlier theories.
items.note: A scientific discovery is a finding or phenomenon established through research.

items.example: A modest technical innovation made the production process considerably safer.
items.note: Technical innovation describes an improvement in the use or design of technology.

items.example: You must enter your PIN before the payment terminal confirms the purchase.
items.note: Enter a PIN means type a personal identification number; avoid speaking the digits aloud.

items.example: Visitors can swipe a card to open the secure laboratory door.
items.note: Swiping involves moving a card through or past a reader; it is distinct from tapping.

items.example: Online banking allows customers to check balances outside branch hours.
items.note: Online banking means accessing banking services over the internet.

items.example: The technician asked everyone to download an app for the demonstration.
items.note: Download an app means transfer and install an application from a network.

items.example: Many people store music on a phone instead of carrying separate players.
items.note: Store on identifies the device holding digital files; this is a practical verb–object pattern.

items.example: Travellers used the Wi-Fi hotspot at the station to check departure updates.
items.note: A hotspot is a place or device offering wireless network access.

items.example: The crew could not get online until the network outage ended.
items.note: Get online is an informal way to say connect to the internet.

items.example: Remote access lets authorised engineers check the equipment without visiting the site.
items.note: Remote access means reaching files or systems from another location.

items.example: We can switch channels without interrupting the television recording.
items.note: Switch channels is the standard phrase for changing the programme source.

items.example: The remote control stopped working when its batteries ran flat.
items.note: A remote control operates equipment from a distance, typically without cables.

items.example: The meeting room has a flat-screen TV for presentations.
items.note: Flat-screen describes the display; hyphenate when modifying TV.

items.example: High-definition TV made the documentary details easier to distinguish.
items.note: High-definition describes increased display resolution, not necessarily screen size.

items.example: The driver relied on the satnav system to avoid road closures.
items.note: Satnav is informal British English for satellite navigation.

items.example: Please switch off a device before disconnecting its power cable.
items.note: Switch off means turn off; a computer may still require a proper shutdown process.

items.example: She decided to download a new app to practise pronunciation daily.
items.note: The natural verb is download, and app is an abbreviated form of application.

items.pt: a televisão ou o meio televisivo
items.example: The documentary director moved from theatre to the small screen last year.
items.note: The small screen means television as a medium, in contrast with cinema.

items.example: The restored film will return to the big screen in December.
items.note: The big screen means cinema or a cinema screen; silver screen is a related idiom.

items.example: The editor checked the expression in an online dictionary before publication.
items.note: Online commonly modifies resources accessed over the internet, including dictionaries.

items.example: The institute created an online course in applied statistics.
items.note: An online course is delivered largely or entirely over the internet.

items.example: There remains a remote possibility that the meeting will be postponed.
items.note: Remote can mean very unlikely, not only physically far away.

items.example: A solar-powered radio network now serves the remote village.
items.note: Remote means distant from populated centres when it describes a place.

items.example: The museum displays tools made in the remote past.
items.note: Remote can refer to a very distant time, as well as distant locations.
